title: Eliphaz Speaks: The Innocent Do Not Perish
summary: Eliphaz the Temanite, the first of Job's friends to speak, begins gently, reminding Job how he has strengthened others and urging him to trust in his own piety. But he goes on to insist that the innocent never perish and that those who sow trouble reap it. He then describes a frightening night vision in which a spirit whispered that no mortal can be righteous before God, who finds fault even with his angels.
story: Job has just cursed the day of his birth in chapter 3. Now the first cycle of speeches begins. Each of the three friends will speak in turn, and Job will answer each one, through chapter 14. Eliphaz, probably the eldest and most respected, sets the tone. He is not cruel; he genuinely tries to comfort. But his words carry an assumption that will harden as the debate continues: suffering is a sign of sin, and the righteous are always protected. The reader, who knows from chapters 1 and 2 that Job is blameless, can see the problem with that assumption before Job does.
historical:
Eliphaz comes from Teman, a region of Edom (Genesis 36:11). Edom had a reputation for wisdom; Jeremiah asks, “Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?” (Jeremiah 49:7). The book presents Eliphaz as a representative of that ancient wisdom tradition, drawing on long observation and even on a claimed revelation.

The friends' view of justice was widespread in the ancient world. Wisdom texts from Egypt and Mesopotamia commonly taught that the gods rewarded the righteous and punished the wicked, and Israel's own Proverbs teach the same pattern as a general truth. Mesopotamian texts about righteous sufferers show that others also wrestled with the times this pattern seemed to fail.
cultural:
Wisdom in the ancient Near East was built on observation and tradition. Eliphaz appeals to what he has seen (verse 8) and to what he has heard in a vision. Night visions and dreams were widely considered channels of divine communication, and the details he gives, fear and trembling, bones shaking, hair standing on end, a form he could not clearly see, and a whispering voice, are meant to give his message authority.

The image of the lion in verses 10-11 was a common one for the powerful wicked, who seem invincible but are eventually broken. The picture of human beings as those who dwell in houses of clay, with foundations in the dust, draws on the idea that people were formed from the ground (Genesis 2:7) and are fragile, easily crushed like a moth. The tent cords being pulled up in verse 21 use the image of nomadic life: a tent taken down in a moment, just as a life can end suddenly.
literary: Eliphaz's speech covers chapters 4 and 5 and is carefully crafted. He opens with courtesy, acknowledging Job's past kindness (verses 2-4), then moves to a challenge (verses 5-6), a principle (verses 7-11), and a revelation (verses 12-21). His rhetorical questions, such as who, being innocent, has ever perished, assume the answer is obvious. The vision account is the most dramatic part of the speech, full of sensory detail and suspense. The message of the spirit is itself a small poem on human frailty. Readers should notice how Eliphaz's gentle start masks a hard conclusion: if Job is suffering, he must not be as innocent as he appears.

outline.t: Eliphaz reminds Job of his past and his piety
No mortal is righteous before God

doctrines.note: The spirit's message is true in itself: no human being is perfectly righteous before God. The problem is Eliphaz's use of it, as a reason to assume that Job's suffering must be punishment for some hidden fault.

Eliphaz claims a revelation, and his words include genuine truths. But the LORD later says the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7). The chapter warns that religious experience and true statements can still be applied falsely.

Human beings dwell in houses of clay with foundations in dust, fragile and short-lived. Eliphaz's description echoes Genesis 2 and is accurate, but the book will show that frailty is not the same as guilt.

words.note: Naqi, innocent, clean, free from guilt. Eliphaz asks, who being innocent has ever perished? The reader knows that Job is exactly such a person. The whole book challenges the assumption behind Eliphaz's question.
Kislah, confidence. Eliphaz asks whether Job's fear of God is not his confidence. He means to encourage, but the implication is that if Job's piety was genuine, it should protect him now.

Tardemah, deep sleep. It is used of the deep sleep God caused to fall on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and on Abram at the covenant (Genesis 15:12). Eliphaz uses the word to claim that his vision came from a sleep of divine revelation.

Chokhmah, wisdom, the skill of living rightly in God's world. Eliphaz ends by saying human beings die without wisdom. Wisdom is the book's central concern, and chapter 28 will ask where it can be found.

christ: Eliphaz's theology, that the innocent never suffer and that suffering reveals sin, is the same assumption the disciples brought to Jesus when they asked about a man born blind: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him” (John 9:2-3). The gospel confronts Eliphaz's principle most sharply at the cross, where the most innocent person who ever lived suffered and died. The link is not prophecy but pattern: Job's story shows the failure of a theology that cannot make room for innocent suffering, and the story of Jesus shows that God himself entered such suffering.

hard.q: Eliphaz says many true things. Why does God later say the friends did not speak rightly?
hard.a: Much of what Eliphaz says is true in general: God opposes the wicked, human beings are frail, and no one is perfectly righteous before God. Proverbs and the Psalms say similar things. The problem is that Eliphaz treats a general pattern as a strict rule and applies it to Job without knowing the facts. He reasons backward from suffering to sin, assuming that because Job is suffering he must have done something to deserve it. The book shows, through the prologue, that this is false in Job's case. Scholars also note that Eliphaz claims divine revelation for his view, which makes his error more serious. Some interpreters point out that Paul quotes Eliphaz's words in 1 Corinthians 3:19 as Scripture, which shows that true statements in the friends' speeches can still be used rightly. The lesson is not that the friends' ideas are wholly false, but that true ideas misapplied can wound and mislead.

questions: Eliphaz starts gently but ends by implying Job is guilty. How can well-meant comfort become harmful?
Eliphaz treats a general truth as a rule without exceptions. Where are you tempted to do the same with your beliefs about God or people?
The disciples assumed suffering must come from sin. What assumptions do you bring to other people's suffering?
